Elements of probability and statistics

Tomorrow there is a 70% probability of rain. A professional scores a penalty in about three out of four cases. And in the newspaper a bar grows that has hardly grown at all. In this chapter you describe random experiments precisely, count frequencies, simulate with the computer, estimate probabilities – and read charts critically.

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • describe random experiments with outcome, sample space and event
  • record data in a raw data list and a tally chart, calculate absolute and relative frequencies, simulate
  • estimate probabilities and calculate them for equally likely outcomes
  • recognise when a chart distorts reality

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Random experiments, outcomes, events

A random experiment has several possible outcomes, and you do not know beforehand which one will occur. Rolling a dice is one, pressing a light switch is not. Everything that can come out is written down as a set.

The set of all possible outcomes is called the sample space $\Omega$ (omega). For a dice, $\Omega = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$. If you group some outcomes together, you get an event $E$, for example “even number”: $E = \{2, 4, 6\}$.

Not all outcomes have to be equally likely. A coin lands on heads almost exactly as often as on tails, but a Lego brick lands much more often on its wide side than on its narrow one.

KEY POINT · RANDOM EXPERIMENT

Random experiment: several possible outcomes, and the outcome is not known beforehand

Sample space $\Omega$: all possible outcomes · event $E$: a subset of $\Omega$

Laplace experiment: all outcomes are equally likely, for example a fair dice

Complementary event: “odd number” is the complementary event to “even number”. Together they make up $\Omega$.

Pierre-Simon Laplace (1749–1827) described the probability for equally possible cases as the proportion of favourable cases.

INTERACTIVE · THE SPINNER

Tap sectors: they form an event. Spin the wheel and count. Switch to “different sizes”: then it is no longer a Laplace experiment.

EXAMPLE 1 · SAMPLE SPACE

A coin is tossed twice. Give $\Omega$ and the event “heads exactly once”.

$\Omega = \{HH, HT, TH, TT\}$, $E = \{HT, TH\}$

4 outcomes, 2 of which belong to E

EXAMPLE 2 · LAPLACE OR NOT?

a) a fair dice   b) a drawing pin: back or side   c) a ticket from a drum of 100 identical tickets

a) yes   b) no, the shape is uneven   c) yes, every ticket has the same chance

a and c are Laplace experiments

EXERCISES

Is this a random experiment? a) drawing a card from a shuffled pack   b) working out $3 \cdot 4$   c) spinning a spinner   d) reading the time

a) yes   b) no   c) yes   d) no

Dice: write as a set. a) prime number   b) greater than 4   c) divisible by 3   d) less than 7

a) $\{2, 3, 5\}$   b) $\{5, 6\}$   c) $\{3, 6\}$   d) $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\} = \Omega$, the certain event

A bag contains 3 red, 2 green and 1 yellow ball. You draw one. Give $\Omega$. Are the outcomes “red”, “green”, “yellow” equally likely?

$\Omega = \{\text{red}, \text{green}, \text{yellow}\}$. No: red is three times as likely as yellow. If you number the 6 balls, it becomes a Laplace experiment with 6 outcomes.

Two dice, red and blue, are rolled. How many outcomes does $\Omega$ have? How many belong to the event “doubles” (both the same)?

$6 \cdot 6 = 36$ outcomes. Doubles: (1, 1), (2, 2), …, (6, 6), so 6.

TEST YOURSELF!

Two coin tosses: how many outcomes does $\Omega$ have?

HH, HT, TH, TT

Dice: how many outcomes does the event “prime number” have?

2, 3, 5

Two dice: number of outcomes?

$6 \cdot 6 = 36$

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Frequencies and simulation

If you repeat an experiment often, you write the outcomes down in order: that is the raw data list, for example 3, 6, 1, 1, 4, … It becomes clearer in a tally chart or a table.

The absolute frequency says how often an outcome came up. The relative frequency is the proportion of all the trials. Only that makes series of trials of different lengths comparable.

Instead of rolling 1000 times yourself, you can simulate the experiment: calculators and computers produce random numbers. In a spreadsheet, =RANDBETWEEN(1,6) gives you a dice number.

KEY POINT · FREQUENCIES

absolute frequency $H$: how often an outcome occurred

relative frequency $h = \dfrac{H}{n}$ ($n$ = number of trials) · all together add up to $1 = 100\%$

Simulation: acting out a random experiment with random numbers

Calculator: many calculators have a key “Ran#” or “RanInt” for random numbers.

Many trials: in long series of trials, the relative frequencies fluctuate less and less.

INTERACTIVE · SIMULATION

Let the computer throw 10 or 100 times. Compare the relative frequencies with the dashed line.

EXAMPLE 3 · FROM THE RAW DATA LIST TO THE TABLE

Raw data list of 20 rolls: 3, 6, 1, 1, 4, 2, 6, 5, 3, 6, 2, 4, 6, 1, 5, 3, 6, 2, 4, 6. How often did the 6 come up?

The 6 came up 6 times. Relative frequency $\tfrac{6}{20} = 0.3 = 30\%$ – clearly more than $\tfrac16$, but 20 rolls are few.

H = 6, h = 30%

EXAMPLE 4 · COMPARING TWO SERIES

Group A: back 52 times in 80 throws of the drawing pin. Group B: back 120 times in 200 throws. Do the results fit together?

A: $\tfrac{52}{80} = 0.65$, B: $\tfrac{120}{200} = 0.6$. Both are close to each other.

65% and 60%

EXERCISES

Count all the scores in the raw data list from example 3 and make a frequency table. Check: do the absolute frequencies add up to 20?

1: 3 · 2: 3 · 3: 3 · 4: 3 · 5: 2 · 6: 6. Sum 20 ✓

In 250 throws, a Lego brick landed on its wide side 115 times. Give the relative frequency as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage.

$\tfrac{115}{250} = \tfrac{23}{50} = 0.46 = 46\%$

Combine the series from example 4. How big is the relative frequency of “back” altogether?

$\tfrac{52 + 120}{80 + 200} = \tfrac{172}{280} \approx 0.614 \approx 61\%$. Do not take the mean of 65% and 60%!

How do you simulate with random numbers from 1 to 6 a) a coin toss   b) a spinner that is half red, one third blue and one sixth green?

a) 1, 2, 3 → heads; 4, 5, 6 → tails.   b) 1, 2, 3 → red; 4, 5 → blue; 6 → green.

Simulate 100 rolls with the interactive element three times in a row. How much does the relative frequency of the 6 fluctuate? What do you expect with 10,000 rolls?

With 100 rolls it usually lies between about 10% and 24%. With 10,000 rolls it fluctuates much less and lies very close to $\tfrac16 \approx 16.7\%$.

TEST YOURSELF!

115 of 250 as a relative frequency (decimal)?

$115 : 250 = 0.46$

6 sixes in 20 rolls: relative frequency in %?

$\tfrac{6}{20} = 0.3$

52 of 80 as a percentage?

$\tfrac{52}{80} = 0.65$

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Probability and reading statistics critically

With a fair dice every number is equally possible. We say: the probability of a 6 is $\tfrac16$. For a Lego brick you cannot work it out – but you can estimate it: the relative frequency after many throws is a good estimate.

For a Laplace experiment you count: probability = number of favourable outcomes divided by the number of all outcomes. Otherwise you estimate with the relative frequency of a long series of trials.

Charts can mislead too. If the axis does not start at 0, small differences look huge. If a picture grows in height and width, it looks much bigger than the number is.

KEY POINT · PROBABILITY

Laplace: $P(E) = \dfrac{\text{number of favourable outcomes}}{\text{number of all outcomes}}$

Otherwise: the relative frequency of many trials as an estimate · $0 \le P(E) \le 1$

Checking charts: where does the axis start? Is the scale even? Does a picture grow in two directions?

Impossible and certain: “rolling a 7” has the probability 0, “rolling at most 6” the probability 1.

Media: a chart never shows reality completely accurately. Always ask who made it and why.

INTERACTIVE · THE AXIS TRICK

Move the start of the axis to 0 and back again: how does the impression change? Switch to “Picture instead of bar” as well.

EXAMPLE 5 · LAPLACE

With a fair dice, how big is the probability of a number greater than 4?

Favourable: 5 and 6, so 2 out of 6.

$P = \tfrac{2}{6} = \tfrac13 \approx 33\%$

EXAMPLE 6 · A CUT-OFF AXIS

Company A sells 520 bikes, company B 500. In the chart, the axis starts at 480. How much bigger does A’s bar look?

What you see is 40 and 20 – A’s bar looks twice as tall. In reality it is only $\tfrac{20}{500} = 4\%$ more.

looks twice as big, is 4% bigger

EXERCISES

Fair dice: calculate the probability of a) an even number   b) 1 or 2   c) no 6   d) a 7

a) $\tfrac12$   b) $\tfrac13$   c) $\tfrac56$   d) 0

A raffle drum holds 200 tickets, 30 of them prizes. How big is the probability of a prize?

$\tfrac{30}{200} = 0.15 = 15\%$

In 1000 throws, a Lego brick landed on its wide side 462 times. Estimate the probability. How often do you expect the wide side in 50 throws?

$P \approx 0.46$. In 50 throws about 23 times.

A newspaper shows the membership of a club: in 2024 there were 300, in 2025 there were 330. The axis starts at 290. How tall does the second bar look compared with the first, and what percentage more members are there really?

What you see is 10 and 40: four times as tall. Really $\tfrac{30}{300} = 10\%$ more.

In a brochure, sales are shown by money bags. Sales have doubled, and the second bag is drawn twice as tall and twice as wide. How much bigger does it look?

The area is $2 \cdot 2 = 4$ times as big. The bag looks four times as big, although sales are only twice as big.

TEST YOURSELF!

Fair dice: probability of a number greater than 4?

$\tfrac{2}{6} = \tfrac13$

30 prizes among 200 tickets: probability of winning in %?

$\tfrac{30}{200} = 0.15$

520 instead of 500: what percentage more?

$\tfrac{20}{500} = 0.04$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

One of the letters of the word MATHEMATIK (German for mathematics) is drawn at random. How big is the probability of an A? Of a vowel?

10 letters, A twice: $\tfrac{2}{10} = \tfrac15$. Vowels A, E, A, I: $\tfrac{4}{10} = \tfrac25$.

The weather forecast says: “70% probability of rain.” It stays dry. Was the forecast wrong?

Not necessarily. 70% means: on about 7 out of 10 such days it rains. On the other 3 it stays dry. Whether the forecast is good only shows over many days.

Two dice: which total score is most likely? Give a reason with the 36 outcomes and state its probability.

The 7: (1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 3), (5, 2), (6, 1), so $\tfrac{6}{36} = \tfrac16$.

EXCURSIONMEDIA

How to lie with statistics

In 1954 the American journalist Darrell Huff wrote a slim book with a cheeky title: “How to Lie with Statistics”. In it he showed how correct numbers can create a false impression.

You now know two tricks from the book: the “gee-whiz graph”, where the axis does not start at 0, and the picture that grows in two directions. Huff also explained why you should always ask: Who counted? How many were asked? What is missing from the chart?

The book became one of the best-selling statistics books of all time. Its aim was not to teach lying, but to help people see through it.

Source: Darrell Huff, “How to Lie with Statistics”, drawings by Irving Geis, New York 1954.
